BasePK: 2407052

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, in discussing this matter with the high commissioner we naturally went into the effectiveness of the economic measures against Rhodesia. The high commissioner is chairman of the economic sanctions committee which was set up at Lagos, and that committee is to meet in London next week. But we have no information which would justify any percentage figure of effectiveness.
We did not discuss any further steps to be taken. That will have to be considered by the committee itself and by the governments concerned, although we did mention the possibility of United Nations action in the security council, under chapter 7, because that has been indicated by one or two members of the commonwealth as being the next step if the economic measures now being taken are not satisfactory.

You are a research assistant analysing speeches from the Canadian House of Commons, 1953-1993.

For each speech, return valid JSON with two fields:

1. `topic`: a short noun phrase, maximum 8 words, describing the main substantive topic.
2. `procedural_score`: a number from 0 to 1 indicating how far the speech moves away from substantive policy discussion toward procedural, partisan, dilatory, or purely formal parliamentary language.

Topic rules:
- Be specific: "old-age pensions" not "social policy"; "railway freight rates" not "transportation".
- Lower-case unless a proper noun requires capitalisation.
- Ignore routine openings such as "Mr. Speaker".
- If substantive content is present, label the substantive topic.
- If no substantive topic can be identified, use "unclear".

Score rule:
- 0 = almost entirely substantive policy, administration, legislation, public spending, economic/social issues, or government action.
- 0.25 = mostly substantive, with minor procedural formulae or partisan rhetoric.
- 0.50 = mixed substantive and procedural/partisan/formal content.
- 0.75 = mostly procedural, partisan attack, obstruction/delay, or formal intervention, with some substantive content.
- 1 = almost entirely procedural, partisan, dilatory, or formal, with little substantive policy content.

Procedural, partisan, dilatory, or formal content includes points of order, privilege, Speaker rulings, adjournment, closure, time allocation, order of business, committee or bill-stage mechanics, divisions, standing orders, unanimous consent, tabling, leave of the House, short formal interventions, repeated objections, delay tactics, or speeches mainly criticising parties, governments, oppositions, leaders, or electoral records instead of developing a policy argument.

When in doubt, give a lower score if the speech contains meaningful substantive policy discussion.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct this question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs on behalf of Canadians of Greek origin throughout the country. Would the government bring to the attention of the President and government of Turkey the serious concern of the Canadian government in respect of the mounting evidence of harassment by Turkey against the ecumenical patriarchate of Constantinople and the forbidding of the archbishop to carry on religious services in the patriarchal church in the city of Constantinople, which in itself would appear to be a serious contravention of the United Nations charter in several decrees and in respect of several agreements which have been arrived at.

BasePK: 2407261

Speech:
Sir, I believe this is a budget involving economic myopia. Only a few short months ago we were in an election campaign. We heard many promises from the present leaders on the government benches. They said "Give us a majority and we shall do wonders".
I would remind these hon. gentlemen of a few of those promises. I would ask the Minister of Finance what provision has been made for the skating rink in Vancouver. What about the $1 million for Digby harbour, or the millions more promised for housing? What provision has been made for the causeways, or I suppose now one might say "pause
April 1, 1966	COMMONS
ways"? What about the $25 million for Cape Breton coal, the dams which have been promised all over the country, the undertaking to provide home mail delivery in small towns, the study of fish which was to be made in Newfoundland, or the $100 million promised for road building in the Yukon-a promise which, incidentally, did not have the effect desired by the government on election day? These are all things which were promised but for which I see no provision made.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
I would be lax in my duty, I feel, if I did not congratulate the minister on his success in the dumping of his predecessor's budget items and the complete reversal of earlier policies both good and bad. "Troubled Canada", Mr. Gordon wrote. "Troubled Walter", Mr. Sharp says. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) lowered income taxes. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) raised them. The hon. member for Davenport put an 11 per cent sales tax on production machinery. The Minister of Finance is timidly removing it. The hon. member for Davenport made much of his billion dollar Canada Development Corporation, which was to have done wonders. The Minister of Finance has forgotten all about it. In fact I suggest Mr. Sharp has forgotten all about Mr. Gordon. In less than a year we have seen a complete switch-round in Liberal direction. We are substituting for the 60 days of decision the present minister's stiletto and 365 days of incision.
I should like to put on record a few extracts to show what sections of the press think about this budget. First I would quote from an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star of March 30:
Mr. Sharp's budget is a shotgun affair which applies to the whole country without regard to regional differences. It ignores the fact that while some regions, such as Ontario have been experiencing a boom verging on inflation, the good times have hardly touched the maritimes and eastern Quebec, where unemployment rates remain far higher than in central Canada. In these depressed areas, the anti-inflation budget could be a recession one.
Then I would quote one or two passages from Le Devoir by Mr. Claude Ryan. I do not think I should burden the house with my French; I have had the passages translated into English and I will read them in English.
While there should be no hesitation in accepting Mr. Sharp's basic outlook in this connection we may well ask ourselves, however, if he has indeed chosen the proper means for the realization of his purposes.
DEBATES	3725
The Budget-Mr. Monteith
In the case of the federal government we should have been able to contemplate a severe reduction not only of spending in respect of construction, but also of the entire spending estimates. Instead of that Mr. Sharp was content to announce a very inconsequential 10 per cent cut in Ottawa's building program. A reduction of approximately $35 millions in total expenses totalling nearly $9 billion is obviously but a drop in the ocean. It may well be wondered what actual effect such a timid move will have on the decisions of other governments as well as on the actual performance of the economy generally. If the federal government really had wanted to set an example it has proceeded very timidly indeed.
Again:
They take no account whatever either of the variety of capital investment problems as they apply to various types of industry nor of the different levels of industrial development as achieved by one area as opposed to another.
And here is an interesting passage:
A year ago the floodgates had been thrown wide open to allow for free play of individual initiative. Since the people were to be called upon to vote they had to be treated as pleasantly as possible. One year later we find ourselves, once again, in the position in which we were before Mr. Gordon's election budget. Whatever Mr. Sharp may say, this is a difference which cannot be explained away entirely by changes in economic circumstances. Its explanation must be looked for, to some extent, in the opportunism of the party in power. If we are now returning to soundly based austerity it is simply because there is no fear of early elections.
Incidentally I think I should put on record the concluding sentence in this editorial:
Unfortunately, nobody thought of encouraging Canadians to invest in their own future, which is perhaps driving short term caution a little iar.
These two editorials give a concise picture of how inept this budget really is. I claim it is leading Canada down the proverbial garden path. I would commend the minister on accepting at least a few elements of the Progressive Conservative party's program. Naturally it is heartening to any political party to find its opponents adopting some of its "policies for people." I refer to the announcement by the Minister of Agriculture offering $4 per hundredweight for industrial milk, which of course was in our program. I refer also to the decision to treat potash solution mining in the same way as any other type of mining for tax purposes. This too was one of our policies. But why did it take so long? Now that parliament has a new senator from that province the government will be able to keep in touch with the needs of the people out there. This is an important decision for Saskatchewan.
The 11 per cent sales tax has now been removed from certain production machinery,
April 1. 1966

BasePK: 2407306

Speech:
I think he was about to rise and say he was not here, thereby blaming his old colleagues for having voted in favour of that.
But, Mr. Speaker, when a country is sovereign and autonomous, when it is really the master of its own destiny, it should not be compelled to do business with private financial institutions. It ought to set up, as a non-profit government body, a public development bank that would finance without interest public expenditures and public development.
This, Mr. Speaker, should be the goal of any sovereign and independent country. But Canada is still controlled by financial interests.
Mr. Speaker, there are in fact two problems facing the country today, or so it seems according to the speech made by the minister.
First, there is the increase in the cost of living. Second, our balance of payments shows a deficit.
The increase in the cost of living, where does it come from and for what reason? Almost everyone tries to hide it from himself and the hon. Minister of Finance especially refuses to see it. But the reason for the increased cost of living during the last year or two is mostly the increase in taxes.

When a province increases taxes by 2 per cent, prices go up 2 per cent. When there is a 1.8 per cent or 1.9 per cent tax increase, as there was last year, prices go up. When the employer is also forced to pay 1.8 or 1.9 per cent more, prices rise. When an 11 per cent tax is charged on building materials, prices inevitably go up.
Through the creation of all sorts of new taxes, we have come to the point where the businessman, simply to make his reports to the government on pensions, health unemployment insurance, income tax for his employees, deductions at the source, taxes on profits, personal income tax, etc., has to hire a whole staff of accountants, secretaries and assistants to figure out all those things and divide everything according to each department. You can imagine that this increases production costs for industrialists and manufacturers contributes to increase prices.
Taxes are the main factor of the rise in the cost of living at this time. The minister complains that the cost of living is on the rise. But he is the first one responsible, for it is not the opposition which raises taxes, but rather the Minister of Finance who decides such things. And as this is the primary cause of inflation, the man responsible for inflation in Canada is the Minister of Finance every time he makes a decision to increase taxes.
Today whether you want it or not, there is 47 cents worth of tax in everything you buy. Every dollar's worth of products includes 47 cents in various taxes, either income, municipal, provincial, school or other tax. In every dollar's worth of production, there are 47 cents in taxes.
The minister wonders what inflation stems from. It stems from taxes or levies, which are higher here in Canada than anywhere else.
The second problem the country has to face is that of the balance of payments. Let us note this however: if we have a deficit, it is not that our exports are inferior to our imports. On the contrary, they are greater than our imports, but over and above that, huge amounts of money go out of the country in dividends, profits and interests paid to foreign companies. That is what causes the deficit in our balance of payments because, as a matter of fact, if we consider only the value of products we ship outside this country and those we bring in, our exports exceed our imports, but we have to pay the tax on money sent to foreign investors who develop our natural resources because we never had a government that could do it.
April 1. 1966

That is why, each year, we send $1.2 billion, I believe-at least, that was the figure two years ago-abroad in the form of dividends, profits and interest.
What does the minister say about that? In his budget speech, he says:
We do not want to restrain export demands-we need the proceeds of exports to pay for imports and meet our very heavy obligations in respect of interest and dividends payable outside Canada.
There you have the heavy obligations: interest and dividends payable outside Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Finance a question: if the United States had enough money to develop their own country, their natural resources, their industries and their trade and if, in addition, they had enough to go and develop natural resources and industries in South America, Africa, Europe, Asia and Canada, can the minister tell us why we Canadians should not be able to find the credit required to develop our own natural resources, our own industries and our own trade like the Americans have done?
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)

BasePK: 2407373

Speech:
That seems to be one of the services for which you receive the honour of being appointed to the Senate.
I believe our universities do a better job of honouring people when they bestow honorary degrees. There are other areas of our life where honours are much more appropriately given, so this is not a good argument for the retention of the Senate.

I have tried to discuss this question today, not in the context of some of the feelings which exist about the Senate. If I had brought down my file of letters, which I have received regarding the Senate, particularly in the last few weeks since certain appointments have been made, this would have produced interesting reading but a different kind of debate. I am asking members to look at this issue, not out of any feeling against any particular Senator over there, or any particular prime minister for the kind of appointments he has made, but in light of what is good for a political democracy and for representative government, which we believe we ought to have in this country.
There are those who suggest that the Senate should be reformed. That has been the cry since 1867. Every prime minister who has tried to reform it has failed, and the methods of reform we have had lately have hardly improved it. I think we should look squarely at it as something not to be reformed, but to be done away with entirely.
There are those who say we should elect our Senators. I suppose that would be better than having them appointed; but I submit that parliamentary government has got along just as well in Manitoba and Nova Scotia without the upper houses that those provinces had at the beginning of their histories. I submit that with all of the strains that we now have in Canada between the federal parliament and the provincial legislatures, between and among our various provinces, it would be just a little too much to have one more strain, namely a conflict between two elected houses which would have, in some sense, equal moral authority, which does not obtain at the present moment.
If the Senate were an elected body, I think it would be in the nature of a fifth wheel, adding nothing to our governmental or parliamentary machinery. For these reasons I believe that we should look seriously at the whole question of whether or not we should keep the other house. It is in this spirit that I have presented this bill today. I have tried not to indulge in personalities or in some of those things we say when we talk about the other place. I ask everyone to look at this bill in terms of what is good for representative parliamentary democracy.
In my opinion it would be better if all those who have a say in the laws which are passed in this country were themselves elected representatives, as they are in this House of Commons. For that reason I ask members
April 1, 1966

to support this proposal for the abolition of the other place.

BasePK: 2407376

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to discuss this evening the matter of our political institutions. As we know, in recent months-in fact, in recent years-the political institutions of this country have come in for some severe criticism. I must say, although I suppose it casts a reflection on some of those who are observers of our political institutions, there has been a noticeable lack of any in-depth analysis of the political institutions of this country. I believe this is unfortunate because I feel that those outside parliament could do more than they are doing to shape and inform public opinion on this very important matter.
We are discussing specifically this evening one aspect of our political institutions, namely the Senate. I think however that in this discussion we ought to bear in mind that our political institutions generally were taken 100 years ago from England. The ideals of parliamentary democracy in England and as they have been developed here are indeed very laudable. I believe however that one is not at all unpatriotic in saying that there may be some serious questions which Canadians ought to be asking about the function of our parliamentary institutions. After all, these
British North America Act institutions in our country were formulated and devised in a unitary state and have been adopted in a federal state which has great regional diversity, and the further complication of being bilingual. Perhaps one of the major weaknesses of our political institutions is that they do not permit an ample and proper reflection of this regional diversity in our country.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when we are talking about the reform or abolition of one segment of our political institutions, really the more serious and pressing question is their analysis in depth. There are two reasons for my finding it difficult to agree with the hon. member who has introduced this bill. One is that if we are to do what he asks today, I think we would not be accomplishing very much in terms of what needs to be accomplished in reforming and re-examining our whole parliamentary institution.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a modest contribution on the motion now before the house as to whether the death penalty, as provided for in the Criminal Code, must be abolished altogether or whether it should be retained.

April 5, 1966
Criminal Code
This question has a high degree of interest for public opinion and is not only controversial, but gives rise to very subjective stands. I am pleased to find that parliament agrees to settle this vital question through a free vote, one which is not subject to party discipline, for it is very binding on each member's conscience.
Mr. Speaker, what are the arguments put forward by the abolitionists? That it is morally wrong for the state, or for a person, to take a human life, in contravention with the Christian principles and human and social rules characteristic of a modern society. That it is a barbaric and outmoded punishment which is not consistent anymore with our modern ethics or philosophy, and most of the civilized countries have successfully abolished it. That the death penalty is but the expression of revenge by society against a murderer, and undesirable.
It is asserted also that capital punishment is not an effective deterrent. It does not have any special deterrent effect as would imprisonment. A great proportion of murders are committed in anger, and then, the consequences have no deterrent effect. On the other hand, whoever plans to escape justice is not influenced by capital punishment. Only the normal, law-abiding citizen could control his impulses when considering the punishment and at any rate, he would not commit murder. The certainty of being discovered and caught has a most effective deterrent effect, and the study of behaviour supports this argument.
It is maintained that a large proportion of murderers are not fully responsible for their actions and that the threat of this or that punishment would therefore not stop them.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a brief summary of the various arguments put forward by the supporters of the abolition of capital punishment.
I have no intention to extend my speech unduly, but I should like to refute those few considerations, and draw from them some conclusions.
The nature of the problem encourages those in favour of abolition to express their opinion openly and dissuades those in favour of its retention from doing the same, because they are afraid to be considered as inhuman or even worse. To justify their stand, those in favour of abolition should demonstrate that capital punishment has proven to be a failure and that it is totally undesirable.

One cannot measure precisely the deterrence of this punishment, but for lack of proof to the contrary, one must admit that capital punishment is a deterrent and, if one is opposed to that punishment, reasons other than lack of deterrence must be invoked. The fact is that we can never know how many people are dissuaded from crime by the threat of punishment, either capital punishment or any other. Since gratuitous murder is extremely bad from a moral viewpoint, punishment must remain severe in order to demonstrate the capital offence it represents against society. Otherwise, the eventual murderer will very likely assume that society does not consider such a crime as one of the most repulsive. Those in favour of the abolition of capital punishment are concerned with saving the life of the murderers and also with the possible result of leading to brutality which executions might have on the people in general. But most, if not all, abolitionists would retain capital punishment if they were convinced it would spare innocent lives. Most feel they would not be justified to endanger the life of one citizen. At a time when the state is losing ground in its fight against crime, we should be more concerned about protecting society than criminals.
Mr. Speaker, let us look at what is going on around us in our respective areas, how many crimes are committed: bank robberies or other robberies, armed robberies, breaking into homes where residents are beaten to death for money alleged to be hidden, rape of young children, indecent assaults, etc.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I feel it would be tragic if capital punishment were abolished to be replaced by life sentence, when we know that our penal and rehabilitation institutions are not now provided with adequate personnel to face the many problems that will arise.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to amend the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act. This act was passed originally in 1935, being chapter 39 of the statutes of that year. The purpose of the present bill is to bring the wages and hours standards in this act into conformity with the standards of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code enacted by parliament last year.
It has been the policy of the federal government for many years to establish wages and hours conditions for work on government construction contracts. This act relates to government construction contracts only. The wages required to be paid are the rates found to be prevailing in the district in which the work is to be performed for each class of

work. The hours standard, however, was specifically set down on a national rather than a local basis. In the act as it now stands these hours are established at eight hours a day, and 44 hours a week, unless longer hours are authorized in special circumstances.
In accordance with the principles which parliament approved last year in the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, the proposed amendment will make it a condition of a federal government construction contract that $1.25 an hour will be the minimum rate to be paid for work on all such contracts if the prevailing standard for any class of work in any area should be less than $1.25. If it is more, the hourly rate is not changed; we want to be sure that it will be brought up to the minimum rate fixed in the Labour Standards Act. If the bill becomes law the standard work week on federal government construction contracts will be 40 hours rather than the present 44, and an overtime rate of time and one half will be required after 40 hours in a week.
Also in line with the hours of work provisions of the Code, contractors will be permitted to work longer hours than under the existing legislation without the necessity of obtaining a permit. At present a permit is required, if it is found necessary to work more than 44 hours in a week. I might say that a substantial number of permits have been issued when work has had to be completed in a short season or in circumstances where completion of a contract was urgent. It is therefore proposed that the act be amended, in accordance with the bill now before the house, to permit the contractor to work up to 48 hours a week without a permit, so long as the overtime rate is paid after 40 hours.

Accordingly an amendment is being introduced in the bill which will require that a construction contract shall contain a provision establishing liquidated damages in case of default in carrying out the wages and hours conditions.

Mr. Chairman, the legislation before us has been anticipated for some time. The proposed increase in the authorized capital of the Farm Credit Corporation from $24 million to $40 million will increase the lending capacity of the corporation and thereby increase the borrowing authorization from $600 million to $1 billion. This is all related to the changes now taking place in the agricultural industry.
The transition that is now taking place in the farming industry is causing an obvious trend toward larger operations. This change in the method or mode of farming has some obviously desirable features but I say with certainty that there are a number of undesirable features as well.
It would not be necessary to increase the amount of loan capital available to the Farm Credit Corporation if we had a better agricultural prices program in this country. Agricultural prices and farm incomes are not
Farm Credit Act
as high as they should be in relation to our economy. For this reason I believe it is incumbent upon the government to do something to increase the amount of farm credit available. Farm operators must enlarge the size of their operations in order to achieve a higher economy. Governments at the federal and provincial level have been increasing the amount of credit capital available to farmers and there has been a steady though not alarming increase in debt on the part of farm operators.
Since it is a fact that our agricultural pricing mechanism is deficient and inadequate, we are not in a position to oppose an increase in farm credit. But we certainly want to say that we have some misgivings in this regard because this is a poor substitute for proper pricing and increased income.
The hon. member for Oxford made a plea to the Minister of Agriculture to amend the legislation so as to increase the size of loans available to farm operators. I suggest that a good deal of consideration and study should be given to the possibility of easing the requirements because many small operators are not able to meet them for the purpose of obtaining credit. These are the people who need capital in order to increase their incomes by increasing the size of their operations. I am sure all hon. members who represent farming constituencies realize that the younger generation of farmers are unable to obtain loans from the Farm Credit Corporation because they cannot meet the requirements laid down by the existing legislation.
In addition to the plea made by the hon. member for Oxford, I ask the government to give consideration to the easing of the requirements under the Farm Credit Act. I realize there must be some limitation because if prudence were not exercised the corporation would find itself in a position of extending loans without security and with little likelihood of repayment. This would be just as harmful to the farmers obtaining these loans as to the corporation itself. In conclusion let me say that with certain misgivings we support this proposed legislation because under present circumstances additional farm credit is necessary for a healthy Canadian agricultural picture.

I promise I will keep my eye on the clock and take not more than seven or eight minutes to complete my remarks.
My colleague has covered much of the ground in his remarks that we compiled for presentation to the commission, and I shall not deal with those areas again. I should like to point out, however, that there was agreement among the political parties regarding the general presentation to the commission when it met in Nova Scotia.
The new boundaries that we propose conform to the municipal lines in the province of Nova Scotia. These are lines which have been in effect for generations and which, of course, determine the set-up of the political organizations. I am advised by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) our colleague from the adjoining riding of Antigonish-Guysborough, that he would have joined us had we asked the commission to take another look at the suggested redistribution of Nova Scotia as it affected the whole province. Unfortunately our efforts were confined to the one county of Halifax, which in the future will have three members and include part of a fourth and fifth riding.
This is perhaps understandable when one realizes that the population served, as of the last census, was 225,723. Halifax, even though a dual riding, is one of the largest in the country. To elaborate on the figures given by my colleague, if the changes were made as have been suggested, creating the Halifax-East Hants riding by adding part of the east shore of St. Margaret's bay and Bedford, the member would represent a population of approximately 77,866, which is within the permissive limitation of 67,000 plus the variation. The riding of Dartmouth-Halifax East, adding the eastern end of Halifax county, would then have a population of 74,950. It should be pointed out that Dartmouth is a growth area so the number would be larger than that. However, we are bound by the figures of the last census.
What effect would these changes have on the adjoining seats from which the proposed areas would be taken? Again we must check the figure for Central Nova and the south shore. We would find that these are still within the acceptable population limits.
The argument has been advanced by my colleague, with the regard to the suggested

April 27, 1966
Redistribution
change, that the area near the head of St. Margaret's bay should not become part of the south shore area but should remain in the proposed Uniacke riding.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
I should like to deal with two other points. First, with regard to the city of Halifax, we suggest to the commission that it do one of two things. The northwest corner of Halifax is taken out to go into the riding immediately west. We suggest that to avoid political confusion the commission follow the ward 7 boundaries in the northwest section of the city. The boundaries determined by the commission have no relation to the ancient ward system of Halifax. Alternatively, if it will not consider making the change to satisfy municipal lines, we suggest that it make the change to satisfy the new provincial lines set up since the commission sat and since we presented our petition. This would be to take out and put in the western riding that area bounded by Windsor street North and Che-bucto, and the Dutch Village road.
There is a population of about 2,000 at the eastern end of Halifax county which we suggest remain in the Dartmouth-Halifax East riding, rather than go into Central Nova. Our submission is that this area is not a viable unit attached to Pictou county and part of Colchester county. There is a crosscountry road between these areas but it is a small one; the major roads in the area run along the coastline. The area has its economic interest identified with Halifax and Dartmouth and its political roots-and politics, of course, are important to Nova Scotians-are tied in with the area immediately to its west.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I would hope the commission would pay some heed to the wishes of the inhabitants of that area and would take a look at the various points we have presented. We have presented them in a non-partisan way, trying to make units as compact and as nearly identifiable with existing units as possible. With those remarks, Mr. Speaker, and with our fingers crossed, we send these speeches to the commission through Your Honour. I would point out that I was right on the dot of seven minutes.

I would add that if one looks up "sub judice" in the index to Beauchesne he will find that this is the only prohibition to which reference is made, namely, that a member cannot refer to a matter on which a judicial decision is pending. I would point out that the question which has been referred to Mr. Justice Spence is one calling for him to inquire fully into certain matters. These things are spelled out. But there is no suggestion anywhere in the order in council that Mr. Justice Spence has to make a judicial decision; he has to inquire into the matters which were referred to him.

It fits in very well with the theory I am trying to enunciate. None of us, as I was saying, can stand aside from the fundamental issues. There is public morality in the tactics we employ. I think we should remind ourselves of this as some of us go about our sinister business. I wonder whether survival unscathed and untarnished will be the only thing to the credit of some of us when we have finished our membership here? What a hollow type of victory this would be. Jacques Barzin answered about another event, when asked what he accomplished in those days, "I survived". Is this to be the sole thing we can say at another time, that we survived? The engines of smear, once started, are hard to stop. The habit of scandal is hard to break. These are days when we should be asking whether there is in fact a decline in the integrity of public life.

No suggestion for the improvement of parliament has been more universally made than the suggestion that we should do more work in committees, and that we should improve our committee work.
The government at the last session of parliament gave some attention to this problem and brought in suggestions and proposals
which, in effect, involved a complete reconstruction of our committee setup. Hon. members know that the names of committees were changed and that a number of other alterations were made. One of the alterations made was to increase relatively the size of the quorum. Under the old rules, under the provisions of standing order 65, the committees had various quorums. They ran at about 30 per cent of the total membership.
In the last session the government deliberately, after much forethought, asked this house to approve that from now on the committees would be smaller in size but would have a quorum of not less than 50 per cent of the membership. There is the provision in the standing orders for the quorum to be reduced under certain circumstances, but that was to be by way of exception.
I suggest that the government asked this house to take a deliberate decision that our committees should operate with a quorum of not less than a majority of the members. The government, in taking this step, in effect stated its view that we should do more work in our committees, and that the committees should do better work. This is a point of view that we all share, and I want to say that I share it too. I think parliament could be greatly improved if we were to upgrade the work done in our committees.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the great reform that was brought in at the last session has not turned out to be such a tremendous reform after all. Committees are having difficulty in getting sufficient members to carry on. Generally speaking they are not making parliament work in the way we thought they would.

I think the work of our committees should be upgraded by having some arrangement whereby they are encouraged to bring in reports, with the assurance that those reports will be considered in this house. I think we should make arrangements, as has been proposed, for committees to sit at times when the house does not sit so those committees can devote their full attention to their work.

I want to ask for your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, and that you turn a deaf ear for a minute and a half while I diverge from the exact point which is in front of us. I realize, as all do, that six years from now another redistribution will take place based on another census. I want to view with alarm for the benefit of the people in Manitoba and Saskatchewan the situation that has developed now and which will be worse in 1971. The point that I made on April 16, 1964, passed unnoticed, I think because there was certain other business in front of the public at that time. I want to make yet another attempt to emphasize this point and I realize you can only do this by repetition. I want to draw to the attention of the people of Manitoba and Saskatchewan the position into which they are being forced through redistribution, and which is going to get worse.
I want to repeat something I said on April 16, 1964, as found at page 2249 of Hansard. I

May 4, 1966
Redistribution
was talking about the discrepancy that was developing with regard to certain areas of our country. I was making an argument which I thought was very sound with regard to area representation in addition to representation by population. I do not know what effect it had. However, I went on to say this:
Here is a major discrepancy which I think we can avoid if we give serious attention to the bill before us and make a proper amendment. Under the census of 1961 the combined population of the four Atlantic provinces was given as 1,897,425.
Now under the distribution of seats to which they are entitled at the present moment they will have a combined total of 32 which gives them a quotient of 59,294. Set that against Manitoba and Saskatchewan. The combined population of those two prairie provinces is 1,846,867 according to the 1961 census-only 30,000 fewer than the population of the four Atlantic provinces. The seats to which they will be entitled under the redistribution now contemplated will be 26 and the quotient per constituency will be 71,033 which is, incidentally, higher than the quotient which has already been estimated for Canada as a whole. Here, with our eyes open, we are establishing a discrepancy between two very important areas of this country. I suggest we should guard against doing so, because why should the Atlantic provinces have 32 seats in this house while the prairie provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan with a population almost the same have only 26? Immediately one finds a variation of six seats as between two of the great areas of Canada. This situation is one which should be examined.
Then, as has been pointed out, we have a somewhat nebulous protection, which I think has been mentioned, for the provinces out there in the absence of a senatorial floor. So by 1971 it is conceivable that Manitoba and Saskatchewan representation could drop from 26 seats to 20 and that the Atlantic provinces would then have 31.
Instead of having a discrepancy of just six seats there will be a discrepancy of 11. That is only one instance where the act has to be reviewed and amended for the future in order that we may not get too far out of line between the various areas of our great country.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the increasing publicity being given to the drug lysergic acid diethylamide, commonly called LSD, I thought it might be appropriate to present a short statement to the house outlining the consideration which is being given to this problem.
The drug in question comes within the category of hallucinogenic drugs which are

being used on an investigational basis in psychiatry. In 1963 the sale and distribution of this drug was prohibited except for small quantities provided by the manufacturer of the drug to institutions approved by the minister for clinical investigation and research.
I would also like to say that there is only one manufacturer of this drug in Canada, and there has been no suggestion that any of the supplies of this drug which have appeared in the illicit underworld market are connected in any way with this company.
It appears that LSD is being smuggled into Canada for illegal sale. In prohibiting the sale of the drug except under the conditions I have mentioned, there was not at that time any thought that the drug would lend itself to illicit trafficking. Developments, however, in recent months have unfortunately shown a growing interest in the drug by persons not under medical care.
The hallucinogenic effects of this drug have received wide publicity, giving the impression that such effects are intensely pleasurable and not in any way harmful to the individual. This is not so. Indeed, this is a highly potent drug, and cases of psychotic breakdown have been reported following its use.
I can assure hon. members that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who are concerned with this problem, are doing their best to eliminate illicit supplies and we have under consideration, in consultation with that force, special measures which will permit more effective control of LSD than is possible under existing legislation.
While I have indicated to members something of our concern over the illicit use of this drug, I would not wish to give any impression that such use is general in Canada, but there is some evidence that it is increasing. It is being used by individuals who choose to experiment with the drug for its special effects without full knowledge of the dangers which could result.
Mr. Speaker, I wished to make this brief statement to the house to indicate that the problem is one which we are actively considering with a view to adopting such measures as will be necessary to deal not only with the illicit traffic in this drug but its illegal possession.

permanent paid position or, alternatively, might cease to exist under that name. Here again such an appointment would only be effective if that position was not a paid position.
At the present time the board invests separately all trusts and funds under its administration. Because of the substantial increase in income which can be obtained by so doing, it is desired to consolidate those of the church's investments which it is not prohibited from consolidating by the terms of the instruments creating them.

Mr. Speaker, the ground with respect to this bill has been pretty well covered
May 25, 1966

in the debate on second reading and I shall not repeat any of the arguments which have been made. However, there is one point that concerns me, and I am glad to have within hearing not only the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson), who I gather is more or less responsible for the legislation, but also the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Favreau) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin). If I may invite their attention to the problem perhaps it may be solved quickly.
As matters now stand, if a person wants to look at the basic law regarding any department of government all he has to do is consult the index to the statutes and he will And there the Department of Justice Act, the Department of Labour Act, the Department of Agriculture Act, the Department of National Health and Welfare Act, and so on.
In the case of the present bill, for reasons which the Prime Minister gave and which carry some weight, several departments are having their basic structure comprised within one bill. It seems to me this will make things a bit confusing in future. I wonder whether the revision of the statutes now in process could cover this point? In other words, what I am asking is in two parts. First, would it be automatic that the commission revising the statutes would take this bill, if we get it through in time, and break it into its component parts so that the general picture I have outlined would still obtain?
Second, if that is not automatic, would there be any impropriety if the minister to whom this commission reports were to make the suggestion to the commission that this be done? I really do not think it is improper because in my own experience I once found an error in the revised statutes and wrote to a minister about it. It was suggested that I pass this information on to the commission.
This matter may be dealt with by a minister rising now in this debate or perhaps it could be dealt with later. I know it is only a small point. Indeed, it is only a technical point, but I suggest it is an important one since the whole purpose of this bill is to make things a bit more efficient. For heaven's sake let us not go in the other direction and find that some of our departmental statutes, which were easily found in the index, have been lost somewhere in an omnibus piece of legislation. I am glad to have the attention of three or four ministers with respect to this point and I would be quite happy to receive an answer from any one of them.
Government Organization

I believe it essent.al that the department to be set up should give leadership in the development of our water resources and in the war against pollution. In order to achieve this result it must be given the tools with which to do the job. The minister must be able to give the necessary leadership. We need to look at the proposed set-up in order to decide whether this can be done under the terms of clauses 29, 30 and 31. I will direct my remarks to clause 31 which deals with the authority granted to the minister of energy, mines and resources.

I have, therefore, read and reread the proposed new subsection 8A of the Resources and Technical Surveys Act to determine the real intention of the government in this respect. The foundation for any real action is lacking. May I illustrate my point by an example.
Senior levels of government can best give guidance by the initiation of pilot projects. In the case of the United Nations agencies, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Development Association, pilot projects are undertaken in developing countries to indicate the essential worth of an agricultural, industrial or educational project. Government Organization operation of them are strictly within the field of the developing nation itself. The pilot project, however, is financed by the international agency to give leadership and impetus to the commencement of such projects.
Likewise, in the fields of water resources and pollution pilot projects are essential. In the Ruhr valley of Germany water resource co-operative associations have been operating since the year 1904. Whole river basins are controlled by one authority and the cost of pollution control is charged directly to those who pollute the stream in proportion to the extent of pollution. The system has been successful in spite of the fact that the Ruhr valley is one of the most highly industrialized and heavily populated areas of the world.
These associations were given almost complete multipurpose authority over water quantity and quality in entire watersheds by their special laws. They have for up to 50 years made comprehensive plans for waste disposal, water supply, flood control and land drainage. Members of the association are principally the municipal administrative districts and the industrial enterprises, and general public supervision is carried out by a government ministry. They have authority to plan and construct facilities for water resources management and to assist their members with the cost of constructing and operating such facilities.

I look, for example, at the proposal with regard to the gradual removal of the sales tax on certain machinery. I ask the minister, if I may, what value is there from the point of view of the productivity of our economy in retaining the sales tax at all?

June 7, 1966

I would like to examine the reasons for supporting such a motion. First, I believe the state should compensate the victims of crime because the state did not adequately protect the citizen from the crime. When citizens gave up their right to carry guns to protect themselves they placed their trust in the state to protect them. It is the state's duty to provide adequate police forces and to have control of arms and other dangerous objects, including automobiles. If the state does not do this and the citizen is injured, then the state must bear the consequences.
Second, if the state does not take sufficient measures to prevent criminal behaviour it should also bear the consequences. The state should take measures to see that certain conditions which breed crime are eliminated, conditions such as slums, inadequate housing, inadequate recreation, inadequate education, inadequate opportunities for employment and inadequate family assistance. If the state does not take measures to eliminate these things then the state should compensate the victims of crime to which these things give rise.

Although the vast majority, about 85 per cent, are in the age group 18 to 25, a number of applications have been received, as I have already noted, from people in their forties, fifties and sixties and it is to be hoped that many people in this age bracket, young in spirit, will find an opportunity to express their social concern through working with the company.
Volunteers will be selected on the basis of their personal qualities, their experience in working with other people and their ability to work effectively in a particular company project. They will take part in a six weeks orientation program before proceeding to their assignments. This program will emphasize aptitudes in human relations, community development techniques, and knowledge of the region and community where the volunteer will work. Once the volunteers are in the field, they will be called together from time to time to evaluate their experience and to take part in further learning sessions. When in the field, they will have the support and advice of people from the agency which is sponsoring their project, other local persons and members of the company staff. They will be granted allowances for food and accommodation, and for expenses appropriate to their projects. They will also receive a small personal allowance. Upon completion of their term of service, they will receive a small honorarium for each month of service.
Any assessment of the impact and importance of The Company of Young Canadians must, of course, await the experience of the first year's program. But we can be reasonably sure about some things. While the volunteer is making a contribution to the social, economic or cultural development of a community, he will also be learning from the people with whom he works. A two-way learning process will be an integral part of every project. If the evidence of similar organizations is any indication, volunteers who serve in the company will leave it as

better citizens, committed to a renewed concern for their fellowmen and a clearer understanding of the processes of change which are so essential to any dynamic and democratic society.
I hope the company, through its volunteers, will have a stimulating, creative effect upon our society and its institutions, and will also help the people of new nations overseas. I believe the company will prove to be an organization deeply concerned with the fundamentals of inequality and poverty in our society and with social justice and democratic progress, and that it will become part of our continuing search for a better Canada in a better world. Bankruptcy Act
the right to apply. The Bankruptcy Act itself defines debtor in section 2, subsection (i). This definition includes an insolvent person.

I know there have been cases which have dealt with the problem of provincial legislation which extended into the field of bankruptcy and insolvency. As one of those who have been directly interested in the motion picture industry in this country for some years, I thought I should like to make a few comments this evening concerning the introduction of this measure to establish a corporation known as the Canadian Film Development Corporation. Like all hon. members of this house, I am in favour of the further development of the arts and culture in our country. I am looking forward to the time when Canada can establish its own identity in Canadian literature, music, art and other things cultural.
However, I have some grave doubts about this resolution so far as the development of a feature film industry in this country at this time is concerned. In the first place, $10 million is a paltry amount in relation to a job of this kind. It is like sending a boy to do a man's errand. Hollywood is the centre of the United States film industry, and with the vast millions that have been put into it, that industry has run into grave difficulties in the last few years. The reason for this has been the impact of television. Television has cut very deeply into this private industry to the extent that in Canada-I have not got the exact figures-hundreds of theatres have had to close their doors. I know that in Winnipeg, the gateway to the west, as a result of the impact of television, no less than 11 theatres closed down in one year.
This does not mean that I am injecting a gloomy note into our discussion. There is still room for motion picture production. However, I feel we have to look at the matter carefully in a young country like Canada that has many more important responsibilities at this time to which reference has been made. It is a curious fact that the minister recently suggested paying $6 million for one painting, but now she suggests an amount of only $10


million for the establishment of a motion picture industry.
The motion picture industry, for instance, is divided into four main branches. First, there are the stars. A few years ago the cost of these stars did not run into too big an item because the motion picture producer could hire a top star on an annual contract. As a result, he might be able to produce anywhere from five to ten pictures with the one star. Now these motion picture stars of top calibre insist on getting into the production end before they will even lend their talents to a production. They usually insist on a contract under which they will make only one or two pictures a year and will take a large share of the profits, sometimes 50 per cent. I do not believe Canada would be in a different position if we were to establish a motion picture industry.
We would find ourselves in the same difficulties as private industry has in this regard. Then, too, these production companies with unlimited millions of dollars behind them have, in the last several years, found it necessary to amalgamate in order to remain in business. Then, you have distribution which is a very important part of the whole motion picture industry. It is all right to produce a picture, but you have to have a whole chain of distribution centres in order to get this film to the next stage, which is the exhibitor himself. All in all, Mr. Chairman, I think we should take a very serious look at this resolution before we support it 100 per cent.

Arthur Rank, one of the great producers of England, came to Canada to look at the potential of this country for the motion picture industry. The province of Quebec-it is nobody's se-cre*

did not yet dare undertake such insurance plans. We are always wondering for what reasons. We mentioned in the committee that the main reason was probably the diversity of cultures in Quebec and particularly the removal or the lack of insurance in the case of truck gardening.
Under the old act, truck gardening was not considered insurable. I believe that by adding this clause, the intention is to make insurance available for truck gardening and the main cultures in the province of Quebec. In my opinion, there is no reference to the volume or density of the crop, but simply to each individual farmer's crop.
There were objections because of the rather small volume of certain production classes in the province of Quebec. I do not understand why, when I find, in other provinces, certain classes whose volume is lesser still than in the province of Quebec, the latter would not seek an agreement with the federal government.

And I feel I should inform the minister that the pressure is being maintained also on the provincial minister.

lost their crops for one reason or another? I am a little apprehensive about what may happen to the prairie farm assistance legislation in the years ahead. If we consider the operation of that act over the period of 27 years I believe we will find that it probably has been one of the cheapest programs in relation to the number of people who have been guaranteed some return. As I say, taking into account the number of years, the number of farmers and the very large area that has been covered, this is no time to be thinking of setting that act aside until we are satisfied that the crop insurance program has developed to the point where it does in fact meet all the objectives which have been laid out.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to round out the roster of speakers for the four Atlantic provinces, that area of Canada which would benefit most by increased trade with the West Indies and a new pattern of trade in
June 22, 1966

that area. It gives me pleasure to second the motion so ably proposed by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) and to speak briefly on it.
First I should like to echo the point made by some of the other speakers, that there is no reason in the world why we cannot pass this resolution before six o'clock because it is in fact a fait accompli. As the last speaker mentioned there will be a conference in Ottawa in July between the Canadian government and officials of the area known as the British West Indies which will deal with the subject matter of the resolution presented by the hon. member for Queens. We need have no qualms that governments are going to fall or be put in impossible positions if we accept the intent of this resolution. As hon. members will recall, the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) had a similar resolution on the order paper some years ago.
Recently in Halifax a three-day conference was held at Dalhousie Univeristy which was supported by the Canadian national commission for the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization and the Institute of Public Affairs of Dalhousie University. It had the blessing and, indeed, the association of the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council. It considered Canada-West Indies relations and the possibility of establishing an institute somewhere in Atlantic Canada. I understand that this possibility is still being studied. We all hope that Atlantic Canada will put its actions where its talk has been in the past. That may sound like a cynical observation, but we have received criticism in Atlantic Canada for talking too much and doing too little in the matter of better relations, trade-wise and otherwise, with the West Indies. I hope we will take the initiative in this regard and show the rest of the country that the words uttered here this afternoon have substance.
I suggest that the British West Indies delegation to the meeting to be held in Ottawa in July will make several concrete proposals, some of which have been developed by Mr. William Demas who is associated with the office of the Prime Minister of Trinidad. His suggestions deal first with tariff measures to improve trade with the West Indies. He suggested at the conference in Halifax that Canada make available more agricultural representatives to assist agricultural development in the West Indies. This, of course, would be a boon to trade between the two
Suggested Promotion of Trade countries. If they grow more they can sell more to us.
The other point I want to make relates to the warning that has been given by the education minister of Barbados, Mr. J. Cameron Tudor. He spoke at the same conference to which I referred and said that a free society will not long be retained in the West Indies if rescue operations are not set in motion immediately.
I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Halifax Mail-Star of Saturday, May 21, which reports Mr. Tudor as
follows:
He warned that the west could not expect the maintenance of the democratic tradition in the West Indies if democracy was unable to get the area out of its economic coils, and added that Canada could play a leading role in assisting the area.
I think there is a challenge here and that if we do not meet it we will be doing a grave disservice to our own country and to an aspiring democratic area which could go the other way unless we ourselves take action. It is with great pleasure, Mr. Speaker, that I second the motion presented by the hon. member for Queens.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, as far as this legislation is concerned, it has been made perfectly clear by various speakers in Her Majesty's loyal opposition that we support the measure in question, though believing there are various changes which should be carried out to make these proposals more effective.
We are greatly disappointed at the absence of any suggestion on the part of the government that an additional $25 a month is to be made available to the old age pensioners of Canada. No one can argue that today, with the cost of living the highest in history, $75 a month meets the elementary requirements of fairness or equity. There are many thousands of people who have been waiting for action, and who from week to week live on a mere pittance, their hopes kept alive by periodic statements that sometime, some where, some place, something will be done.
Today, I intend to review the stand which we, as the opposition, have taken on this matter throughout the last couple of years. I make no apology for going into detail, and I resent very much the suggestion of the minister that there has been on the part of the opposition an attitude of filibustering this bill. As far as the Conservative party is concerned, representatives from all the provinces, I think, have made their views clear. They have the right and duty to do this.

The minister in a moment of annoyance, I think, decided he would brand the opposition as being responsible for a filibuster, thereby taking the pressure off the government for action on behalf of the old age pensioners. Just after he spoke the other evening in this regard I decided to look up the meaning of "filibuster". In the old days in parliament speeches of seven, eight, nine or ten hours were not unusual. Those days, of course, are past. I recall I used to get Hansard in 1910. I was greatly impressed by a member by the name of Mr. Lafortune who, at the end of 14 hours, told the Speaker that he was "about to come to the essential portion" of his argument.
I recall very well that in the days of Prime Minister Mackenzie King speeches on occasion were of almost limitless extent. No one suggested that Mr. King would engage in a filibuster against himself and his party. Mention is sometimes made here of Senator Wayne Morse in the United States. I find that on one occasion he spoke for 22 hours and 26 minutes; he was excelled in length only by a member of the legislature of Texas who spoke for 28 hours and 30 minutes.
Filibusters are in the nature of speeches made without any objective in mind except to hold up the passage of legislation by the government. It is not a filibuster to demand from the government justice on behalf of the old age pensioners of Canada.

The most compelling and unanswerable statistic that I have found in my study of this problem is printed at the bottom of page 10 of the Anal report of the special committee of the Senate on aging. It might be assumed by a good number of Canadians that older people would have the advantage of some assistance from their families. Yet paragraph 3 of
Canada Assistance Plan this report, at the bottom of page 10, point out that in 1961 there were 570,000 of what are called unattached persons, that is, widows, widowers or older people whose children have moved out, over two-thirds of them women and that their median income on the basis of non-farm sample was $829, with 60 per cent receiving less than $1,000 annually. In an aside the report says that we know less than we should about how these people manage.
An even more compelling statistic is that of the remainder, some 252,000 persons, 63 per cent of them were women living alone or with non-relatives, and were presumably dependent for the most part on their own resources. Of this latter group 53 per cent had incomes of less than $1,000, and among those age 70 and over 47 per cent of the men and 50 per cent of the women received almost their entire incomes in the form of old age security pensions. Thus we have a figure of approximately 130,000 people with no other income than $75 per month.
It is generally accepted that one-quarter of one's income should be spent on providing a roof over one's head. But for people in this category a generous nation suggests that $18.75 or $19, not to cut it too finely, is sufficient to spend monthly on accommodation. Where is it possible to get accommodation at such a rent in Canada today?
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
It has been suggested by various members who have taken part in this debate that if we pass the Canada Assistance Plan, permitting the federal treasury to enter into partnerships with the provinces which could vary from one end of Canada to the other, we will be applying different standards to help our elderly people in need, depending upon the provinces in which they live. This is quite obvious.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) also drew our attention to the great difference in municipal welfare services across Canada. It could be pointed out that voluntary welfare services provided by agencies which exist in different parts of Canada also do not cover the whole country. We have the Red Feather appeals in metropolitan, city and town areas but no help is provided in many parts of the country by those agencies covered by the Red Feather campaigns. I think this argument tends to snowball in favour of something being done in a dramatic and even generous way by this parliament so that we



July 4, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan do not write off many members of a generation who are unable because of their age to look after themselves.
At page 11 of the Senate report to which I referred earlier there is an interesting table giving the percentages of non-farm population 70 years of age and over with annual incomes of less than $1,000, by sex, age, and marital status. Just dealing with one group, the male group, for the year ended May 31, 1961, the figure for those from 70 to 79 was 37 per cent, from 80 to 89 it was 58 per cent and for those 90 and over was 62 per cent.
One could go into the impelling needs brought about by advancing age, medical assistance and perhaps special foods. The costs of these are mounting inexorably and income is declining drastically. This situation is simply not fair to older Canadians.
Let me make a final point to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) in view of my familiarity with the area from which he comes. They are very proud people and I am sure if the minister went to their doors and attempted to explain a needs test as opposed to a means test he would not receive a warm welcome.
I am sure that the minister could look about the villages of his constituency and find that many of the people would sooner deprive themselves of the extra help that could be provided under a formula tied in with a test, deprive themselves of the necessities of life, rather than go through the humiliation of filling out such a form. I am sure there are hundreds of people in Inverness-Richmond who have that feeling. I know from my own mail that there are thousands in my particular area who feel that way.

Mr. Chairman, I think we recognize, too, that while an individual's health is a highly personal affair in many respects, his or her good health is of direct benefit to the wider community.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
These are the fundamental points which I believe every Canadian can and does support. The question is how best we can assure that this goal is met. The federal government's proposal, as hon. members know, is to offer the provinces a sizeable sum of money to support provincial medical care insurance programs which meet certain established standards.

July 12, 1966
Health and Welfare
We have taken this approach because we recognized that under our constitution health is a provincial responsibility and, because of this, federal initiative in this field is limited to encouraging provincial action. This is an important point, but one which I am afraid has been lost sight of in some of the debates on this subject.
It would be much simpler and, to some, more attractive to shunt these considerations aside and promise broad and direct federal action in this field. But in practice this would amount to little more than an exercise in futility, for it would mean making federal promises that are not within the federal power to keep.
It may be a matter of interest to members to note the manner in which changing times and conditions are reflected in the varying methods by which federal assistance has been made to provincial programs in the unfolding of our health insurance plan. When the health grants were introduced in 1948, many provincial governments were financially hard-pressed and because of this condition, but at the same time respecting the constitutional position, the federal government set up a series of health grants only some of which required the matching of the funds by a province. Thus, for many years in certain areas, the federal government has been providing through some of the health grants payments in full for projects designed and administered by the provincial governments.
By the time the hospital insurance program was introduced, federal sharing had become the usual means through which the government of Canada made contributions toward programs which clearly fell within provincial jurisdiction. Thus, the hospital insurance program became a conditional grants program under which the federal government began providing very considerable sums of money, but only with respect to shareable items of expenditure approved by the provincial governments.
The present phase of health insurance comes at a time when the conditional grants technique is undergoing some rethinking. Hence, it would not be in conformity with this policy to bring in a measure designed along the lines of existing conditional grant programs.

To have recalled parliament before the decision to strike was made would have been taken, of course, as a proclamation by the government that there was no hope of any kind of a settlement between the parties, and it would have represented an interference in an unprecedented way with the collective bargaining process laid down by our law.
Once the strike date was set the government lost no time in calling parliament. We acted on the same day. We knew, of course, that in doing this we were making further bargaining and mediation more difficult, but we knew also that there were only four days for mediation before the date that was set for the strike.

There are also those, Mr. Speaker, who say
we should have had parliament meet on Thursday of last week so we could ask parliament to prevent the strike by legislation. Naturally that course was considered. It has been followed in the past. Apart from the fact that the time was so short between the calling of the strike and the date for the strike, to attempt to legislate last week in the circumstances of that week, to attempt to legislate before Friday noon in our view was not likely to have been an effective course for achieving the objective in mind.
We should not forget and I am sure we do not forget, Mr. Speaker, that under our laws the union leaders have an undoubted right to call a strike and the employees have an undoubted right to go on strike. They are acting, in doing so within the law, as I am confident they will continue to act. We should not forget and we do not forget that the right to strike is a cherished and integral part of our system of free collective bargaining, and neither government nor parliament should abridge, or would want to abridge, that right without the strongest reasons of national interest and public welfare, and not until every effort of persuasion and mediation has failed. This is why we felt that a final attempt at mediation even after a strike date had been set, under the auspices of the Minister of Labour, was not merely justified but was necessary in the public interest. That final mediation did not, unfortunately, avert the strike; it is continuing as we sit in this chamber.
Two alternatives faced the government, as they faced the country. We as a government could have abided by the ordinary law and allowed the strike to continue until the parties finally came to an agreement on their own with all the assistance the government could give them. Or parliament could be asked to intervene on the ground that a promulgation of the strike would do such great harm to the public interest, including the interest of the parties to the dispute, as to constitute a national emergency which justified a departure from ordinary practice and law.
We had no difficulty in deciding that it was our duty as a government to follow the latter course as now being necessary to restore an essential public service with the least possible delay and to get the railways moving again with the least possible interference with the process of free collective bargaining. Mr. Speaker, earlier in the debate the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) (Mr. Danforth) outlined the position which the Conservative party takes on this bill. I agree completely with the points he presented to the house. For this reason it will not be necessary for me to repeat the points which he so ably brought to our notice. But I wish to speak for a few minutes on behalf of the Ontario producer of feed grains who wishes to ship his product to the Atlantic provinces.
We in this party favour strongly the freight rate subsidy which is paid on feed grains produced in western Canada and shipped to eastern Canada, because it helps the western producer of feed grains to sell his product. The subsidy is also of great assistance to the eastern feeder in keeping his costs of production at a reasonable level, thereby making it possible for him to sell his product to the retail consumer at a reasonable price. This is something which is most important at this time of rapidly rising costs and prices in all parts of the country.
In all fairness, I believe that something must be done to assist the Ontario producer of feed grains selling to the Atlantic provinces in exactly the same way as we assist the producer of these same feed grains in western Canada in selling to the Atlantic region. We ask no more, but we demand no less. That, Mr. Speaker, is only fair play.
As the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) ably pointed out a few moments ago, there are instances where the shipper of feed grains, shipping from some point in Ontario to some point in the Atlantic provinces, pays a freight
Canadian Livestock Feed Board rate six times as great as that paid by the producer of these same grains in western Canada. We in Ontario want no more and no less than similar producers in western Canada receive. We think that the subsidy paid on the grains being shipped to the Atlantic provinces is completely fair. We have always spoken in favour of that subsidy and we always shall. But we want an equalization of freight charges on feed grains produced in Ontario and shipped to the Atlantic provinces. This will in no way hurt the producer of feed grains in western Canada. It will be of considerable assistance to maritime feeders because in this way they will get corn, which is becoming an increasingly important feed in all parts of the country today, at a lower rate than they are at present having to pay.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, there is no appreciable amount of corn grown in western Canada. Certainly, none is grown for export. All feed corn grown in western Canada is used for feeding in that region. If Ontario corn receives the same freight rate assistance that other feed grains from western Canada at the present time receive, feed grains that are being shipped to the Atlantic provinces, the maritime feeders will be provided with cheaper feeds for their cattle, which will be of great benefit to them.
[DOT] (1:20 p.m.)
It is interesting to note that today the annual increase in the production of feed grain in Ontario amounts to more than the entire production of this product only eight years ago. I therefore strongly urge the minister to recommend to his colleagues the equalization of freight rates on feed grain moving between western Canada and the Atlantic provinces as well as on feed grain produced in Ontario and shipped to the Atlantic provinces.
This is fair treatment for the Ontario feed grain producers. It in no way hurts western producers and it will be of material assistance to feeders in the Atlantic provinces because they will be able to buy Ontario grain more cheaply than they are doing so at the present time. In my opinion it will be of great benefit to all concerned while inflicting hardship on no one. I believe the recommendation I have made should be seriously considered by the government. I hope they will give it such consideration and bring in an amendment to this bill along those lines.

Canadian Livestock. Feed Board transporting it.
