Speech:
Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to have heard the discussion that has taken place because some time ago we who served on the agricultural committee were impressed with the manipulation and manoeuvring of some people in the province from which the hon. member for Megantic comes. There is some merit in considering things that have happened in the past and devising ways and means of eliminating them in the future.
One thing which has not been mentioned much is the relationship between the Canadian Wheat Board, which is the sales
October 11. 1966

Canadian Livestock Feed Board agency of the western farmer, and the livestock feed grain board which has a purchasing function. Another important matter which was raised in the agricultural committee, during the time the Liberal party was opposed to this type of proposed agency, was the necessity of maintaining equilibrium between the cost factor for the production of western beef and other meat products and that same factor in eastern Canada.
That is a factor which most members of the committee were desirous of maintaining. We do not want this new board to sell grain in eastern Canada at a price much more advantageous than that being paid for grain in western Canada, thus creating a disparity between the two types of production, which in turn could only lead to an elimination of one of the boards, either the wheat board sales agency or the purchasing agency of the livestock feed grain board.
This is something which the advisory committee will have to examine more than once a year. When it knows production levels in western Canada it can relate them to needs in eastern Canada. The number of cattle in each area will be a large determining factor in the amount of purchases which the board will make. For these reasons the minister would be well advised to amend clause 15(3) by deleting the words "shall meet at least once a year" and substituting therefor the words "at least four times a year".
This board will have to make decisions at the beginning of each crop season and again in the fall of the year when the availability of grain is determined. It will also have to determine the amounts of grain to be stored, and in order to maintain the differential between east and west it should review the situation at fairly frequent intervals. If it does not, then one part of Canada will be unhappy and very likely that part will be western Canada.
The minister has said that there will be representatives on the committee from all areas. I hope this is true and that included among them are the areas of beef production in western Canada which have a great stake in the effects of this legislation and should play a primary role in an advisory capacity in maintaining what we believe is a reasonable status quo. Therefore I move as an amendment to clause 15(3), line 11, that the words "at least once a year" be deleted and the following words substituted therefor, "at least four times a year."

Those are Mr. Hellyer's words. The minister was speaking about me and his statement clearly imputes an improper motive. His words are so strong as to impugn my very honour and integrity.

Having made the charge, I could have merely sat down at that point, but naturally when very serious matters are at stake we try to assist the house in finding a way in which the matter can be dealt with.
The reason for not going further was simply the procedural difficulties which I have been unable to overcome. I would remind the house that on Wednesday, October 12 these difficulties were almost overcome but the minister, who as an honest gentleman should have been looking for a way to have the matter investigated so that his name could be cleared, was the only member in the house to refuse unanimous consent which would have made it possible for this matter to be investigated.
Then on Thursday, October 13 the minister, having barred further consideration of this matter, made some statements against me which caused me to rise on a question of privilege suggesting that he was attacking my motives. Your Honour will remember that when you dealt with this matter on Thursday the minister got up and made a statement which in my opinion did not clear the minister of imputing motives; but Your Honour, on considering the matter, said the following:
My limited experience in the house indicates that it is not per se, unparliamentary to say of another member that the statement he makes is false, untrue, wrong, incorrect or even spurious, unless there is an improper motive imputed-

The minister has taken the opportunity to do what I would have asked him to do in any event, to say that he did not impute motives.
Mr. Speaker, I contend that it is no longer open to the minister to suggest that he was not imputing motives. He made the statement to the press expressly for the purpose of imputing motives.
The manner in which he made that statement makes it quite obvious that he was imputing motives.
I would ask Your Honour to rely on the statement with which you ended your ruling that I did not have a prima facie case of privilege, which appears at the top of page 8599 of Hansard:
I realize that in some instances words may be used which are so strong as to impugn the very honour and integrity of the individual member against whom the words are directed.

He has gone even further and said that I am proceeding with the case only to embarrass him.

I ask Your Honour to rule that I now do have a prima facie case in this matter.

Question of Privilege

[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Today, on second reading of Bill C-227, I want to add a few thoughts after having heard other speakers, and especially after having noticed the complete silence of the federal ministers from Quebec, when this legislation does great injustice to my province which has decided, and rightly so, not to participate in it.
To my knowledge, only one minister, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), commented not in this house but during a radio program on the French network of the C.B.C., between 9.15 and 9.30
Oclober 20, 1966

a.m., on October 18, 1966, the position I took in the house last Thursday night and Friday. In his remarks, the minister assured the whole French speaking audience of that network throughout Canada that the federal legislation on medicare respects provincial autonomy and that the purpose of the four conditions inserted in the federal act was to ensure equal treatment between the provinces.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I want to refute once again those false statements which deceive the Canadian people, and are mere window-dressing, to make them believe that provincial autonomy is respected even though provincial rights are thoroughly violated. The autonomy of the provinces exists not only in the rights granted to the provinces but also in the financial means they need to exercise them. By laying down four conditions, Ottawa is interfering with the freedom of choice of the provinces; by refusing to hand back enough taxation fields to the provinces, Ottawa weakens and reduces financially the exercise of provincial rights.
Therefore, that federal medicare legislation does not respect at all the autonomy of the provinces as far as their rights and their financial means to exercise them are concerned. To maintain that this federal legislation respects provincial autonomy is to deceive the Canadian public on the meaning of autonomy of the governments in a federative system, to oppose flatly the Quebec point of view and to show the most centralizing attitude.
To say that the four federal conditions are designed to strike a balance between the provinces is to want Ottawa to act as a substitute at all times for the initiative and intelligence of the provinces. The provinces hold annual interprovincial meetings and they are able to agree and work out their legislation. They do not need a systematic and omnipotent intruder.
If some provinces are too poor, the others can set up between themselves an assistance fund. To use constantly that balance as a argument is to perpetuate the best reason for federal interference and encroachment. That systematic presence of Ottawa is creating such imbalance, tension and discontent. That presence of the central government in provincial fields of jurisdiction goes against the existence of a truly federal union and is proof of the legislative union towards which Ottawa is rapidly moving.
Medicare
What is most unfair in the federal medicare legislation is its immediate refusal to grant the tax admustment to the provinces which will decide to opt out.
The practical result of that refusal will be an annual loss of millions of dollars for a non-participating province and, in addition to supporting a provincial medicare scheme, the citizens of that province will have to pay to Ottawa taxes which will be spent in the other provinces.
It is unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration made such a choice and should now praise centralization. By so doing, he completely disowns the aspirations of the province he comes from. Moreover, in so far as Quebec is concerned, be becomes a stranger, an opponent.
Through his attitude toward the bill on medicare, the hon. Minister of Manpower and Immigration finally reveals what he thinks about federal-provincial relations. He proves to be, just like his other colleagues in the cabinet and other Liberal members from Quebec, a true centralizer. Before being elected to parliament, he claimed he was going to Ottawa to save confederation. How can he try to save the confederation when he agrees, here in the house-and when he has definite responsibilities-to all kinds of infringements of the constitution and encroachments on provincial rights? I find instead that like his other colleagues-and I am speaking in this house as a free man-he is only trying to save his own skin and preserve his eventual leadership for the federal Liberal party.
I want to express today my deep disappointment, as well as that of thousands of people in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, in order to redress the injustice of the federal medicare legislation which does not provide for a fiscal compensation, I move, seconded by the member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), that all the words after "that" be deleted and that the following be substituted therefor:
This house, while of the opinion that the necessary steps should be taken to ensure that appropriate medical services are made available to all Canadians, nevertheless believes that no legislation providing for insured medical services in Canada would be adequate unless it provides for a system of fiscal compensation for any province desiring to set up its own autonomous medical insurance plan.

complete, detailed explanation of just what happened in this regard.
Having regard to the other part of the Prime Minister's statement, which I find remarkable, the facts I have received do not bear out the propositions he put forward about discussions on the question of integration and unification. I refer particularly to the discussion of unification by the committee on national defence. A lot of the information given created a completely false picture in so far as the activities and the opportunities of that committee are concerned, having in mind the feeling of the Minister of National Defence in this regard.
We have also noted the smokescreen created by the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of National Defence, who have suggested that our present attitude was carefully adopted because we were holding an annual meeting. As a matter of fact, as far as I am concerned, the opposition to the government's stand on this matter was as valid this past week as it would have been two months ago and as it would be two months from now. This whole question involves a matter of principle. The minister told us last June that no decision had been reached with regard to this whole proposal.

There were 2,300 pages of testimony taken.

This was back in 1953 or 1954. We should change this attitude. We are a country which can start a world food bank by making available our resources for this purpose. In this area leadership from a country such as Canada would supply the impetus to proceed from mere discussions to active accomplishment.
The same is true in general about aid to the developing countries. As has been pointed out in various debates, Canada's contribution to the developing countries at the present time is a niggardly one. It is away below the 1 per cent which is our present objective in the United Nations. It has seemed to be a larger figure because our grants and also our loans and credit arrangements are included in the amount. Our actual contribution, as distinct from credits and loans, amounts to about one third of 1 per cent of our gross national product. Here is an area in which instead of merely engaging in discussions with others and regretting the insufficiency of aid to developing countries, we could give leadership by increasing our own aid to an adequate level.

I conclude my remarks in the hope that Canada will act so as to give leadership to other countries through the development of new policies in these areas.

This paragraph gives us an opportunity, for the first time, to deal with the whole question of federal-provincial relations both with regard to the legal position and also with regard to the wisdom of the federal government attempting to do what is being done here, bearing in mind the precarious state of relations between the two senior levels of government.
To consider this subject adequately, we must take into account the background picture of relations between the federal government and provincial governments as they have developed over the last two or three years. I will simply say, in passing, that the attitude of the present government in that period has been so sinuous and winding that it would break a snake's back to follow it.

December 1, 1966
Medicare

First, firm action was taken. Then came co-operative federalism, which really was another euphemism for complete yielding whenever a crisis situation arose, whenever there was a conflict. Finally there came the last stage, which we are in now, this apparent determination to intrude into matters which are strictly ones for the provincial governments.
I am not suggesting, and I do not want my argument to be taken as suggesting when looking at the definition of "participating province", that essentially a scheme of this kind might not in the final analysis be best under the control of the federal government. If the founding fathers, 100 years ago, had any idea as to the extent to which it would be necessary to interfere with social and economic conditions of people, I am quite certain they would have allocated to the federal government the sole responsibility in matters of this kind. But they did not, and we have to deal with this matter as it now stands. We have to consider whether "participating province", which leads us to a consideration of clauses 3 and 4, is something which should be dealt with in the context of this bill.
I point out to the committee, Mr. Chairman, that there is first the direct conflict, the constitutional issue per se. The minister yesterday quite properly said to me, when I asked him a question following his intervention on a point of order, that he would deal with this point in its proper place. I suggest this is the proper place to put on the record his views and the views of the government. But, as a brief foundation for what he might say, I want to point out that I do not think it is a subject which is entirely free from doubt.
The nearest approach to a scheme of this nature, I think, is the scheme with regard to payment of family allowances. This was tested in the courts, so far as I can recall, on one particular occasion, as a matter of fact when the government was introducing its legislation in connection with student loans. At that time I approved the attitude and the actions of the government. I spoke on the resolution stage, and on the bill itself, and I referred the house at that time to this particular case, which was a Quebec case, and which I think was a judgment of the Supreme Court.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I posed a question to the Postmaster General (Mr. C6te) with regard to what I termed rather poor mail service in the province of Nova Scotia. At that time I referred to the fact that the Western Catholic Reporter takes two weeks to reach Nova Scotia from Edmonton, Alberta. This is what has been happening in the past. This is what I am doing at this time. In fact one of the clergy advised me that one issue of a newspaper printed three weeks ago had not arrived yet. He had written the editor of the newspaper in Kingston and in reply was told that it had been mailed very early.
Rather than go into great detail I should like to read an editorial and put it on record. It appeared in the Antigonish Casket, a newspaper published in Antigonish, Nova Scotia, on November 24,	1966. It is entitled
"Threatened Postal Strike" and reads as follows:
Most Canadians must have breathed a sigh of relief last week when the threatened postal strike was averted. We have maintained before, and we repeat our belief, that postal workers have a right to strike even if this should mean considerable disruption in the lives of all Canadians. We do, however, feel that there is something gravely wrong in the Canadian postal service.
Our own experience would indicate that the department spends far too little money to provide a really adequate postal service in the province of Nova Scotia. With practically all of the mail within the province transported by truck rather than by

train, the trucking service is entirely inadequate both as far as accuracy of sorting and frequency of deliveries are concerned.
Before the trucking service was introduced one New York magazine-not a news magazine incidentally-used to reach Antigonish on Monday following its Saturady publication date. Recently, however, we received the November 5 issue of this magazine on November 12, it was followed on November 14 by the issue of October 29 and on November 15 by that of November 12. To take another example, our copy of the National Catholic Reporter of November 2 reached us on November 15; the copy of November 9 arrived on November 16.

Another very notorious example of the complete inadequacy of the present system is the delivery of the Sunday New York Times. This used to arrive in Antigonish on Tuesday almost without fail. Now we hardly ever get it before Wednesday; very often it arrives on Thursday; occasionally it comes on Friday. Surely we have occasion to complain when a newspaper takes from Sunday to Friday to come from New York to Antigonish.
As far as letters mailed within the province are concerned we have equally grave objections. For news stories from the Cape Breton area we rely on telegraph service, but occasionally we need pictures from the Sydney area rather urgently. A picture mailed in the main post office in Sydney on Saturday, however, usually is not delivered in Antigonish until the following Tuesday. A letter mailed Monday morning at the Sydney post office very seldom makes our printing deadline of Tuesday noon.
The root cause of the whole problem is that the Post Office Department will not spend enough money to provide adequate service in Nova Scotia. As in so many other things. Nova Scotians are being shortchanged by their government in Ottawa,
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to pay particular attention to that sentence in the editorial, which I should like to repeat:
As in so many other things, Nova Scotians are being shortchanged by their government in Ottawa.
It is of great importance that Postmaster General Cote and his staff recognize the problem, and to do something about the postal system that is crumbling-at least in Nova Scotia.
I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, knowing the Postmaster General as I do and, as I said this afternoon, having always found him a gentleman in all matters, that he will give this matter his serious consideration and perhaps investigate the problem. I wish to thank him for doing me the courtesy of remaining in the house this evening. I know he is a busy man and could possibly be doing other work but it is an indication of how serious the minister feels the situation is. I hope he will say a few words with reference to this problem so that I can reply to the publishers of this editorial in the Antigonish Casket, as well as to the clergy and other subscribers affected.

advisory committee has been judiciously mixed, consisting of those who are producers and those concerned in the processing side of the industry, in order to try to give the Dairy Commission balance between the respective interests of producers and processors.
There is one matter that he mentioned near the end of his remarks that I should like to underline, and ask the minister to take under serious consideration, Mr. Speaker. He mentioned something about scepticism and cynicism in the handling of dairy problems. I think it is fair to say that, next to the problem of the vast number of farmers in Canada who have still not come up to the minimum standard of living for Canadians is the problem of the dairy industry.
The fundamental problem that is facing this industry is the divided jurisdiction between the federal government and the provincial governments. The key to the problem will be in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. Because of the fact that goods can flow back and forth between those two provinces so easily, one of the priority tasks of the Dairy Commission will be to get the two provinces which are the major producers of dairy products to agree on some form of marketing arrangement whereby liaison between these two provinces is sufficient to extend the same conditions to producers in both provinces, and to work together to resolve the general difficulties of marketing on the whole of the national scene. The Dairy Commission itself by its very nature should consider this a prior task.
The minister also indicated that one of the jobs would be the handling of the marketing throughout the world of dairy products produced by the industry in Canada. This is of course the major weakness of the dairy industry today in Canada. Traditionally the industry launched its markets toward the cities around which were the milk sheds. This orientation toward the city markets is long overdue for change. The world is in desperate need of proteins, and if the industry is organized properly these proteins can be sold on the world markets. Instead of the dairy industry going downhill, as it has been going for many years, that industry could be one of the main weapons of the Canadian people, using our tremendous production potential to feed the hungry peoples of the world. That objective should be one of the major tasks of this Dairy Commission.
I think the minister is quite right, and I hope he has repented of his sins when he

implies that there should not be political concepts in the resolving of the dairy industry's difficulties. If you bring partisan politics into the problem of resuscitating and rebuilding this important industry, every move is doomed to fail. This is not an area in which to start fights on this subject among provincial ministers of agriculture, or between provincial ministers and the Minister of Agriculture.
This subject must be dealt with on a purely economic basis, not only for the good of the milk producers in Canada, but for the good of the task that we all have, which is to help to feed the hungry world which desperately needs the proteins of this industry.

Mr. Speaker, the urgency arises because, first of all, the house will have no further opportunity, except through a motion for adjournment, to discuss such a matter. As all supply motions have been passed and as there are no more interim supply bills to examine, we will have no further opportunity to deal with this matter until next year.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) recently issued a press release to the effect that, again this year, ice-breakers on the St. Lawrence will not be commissioned to clear the seaway for shipping, but will simply prevent ice-jams and floods occurring in the spring.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, to show that this is a definite matter of urgent public importance, let me remind the house that last year 120 ocean-going ships reached Montreal and that 200 are expected to this year. However, if the St. Lawrence river is not cleared, it will hamper and interfere with winter shipping. It is urgent that the matter be discussed without delay and that decisions be taken as soon as possible, so that shipping companies, knowing that the St. Lawrence river will not be open to shipping again this year, will not plan to use that great seaway. If we now have a fruitful discussion on the problem and if the Minister of Transport is in a position to announce that ice-breakers on the St. Lawrence will clear the way for ships to reach the port of Montreal, shipping on the St. Lawrence will increase as well as port operations at Montreal, for the benefit of the whole country.
A debate is most urgent, Mr. Speaker, as is evidenced by the fact that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) intends to ask leave to have a special sitting of the house tomorrow morning to deal with the matter of the west coast tie-up due to a strike.
The port of Montreal and those along the St. Lawrence are closed because of ice conditions and the Minister of Transport can easily put at the disposal of the authorities of those ports the icebreakers required to ensure year round navigation on the river.

Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the cases are similar: on the one hand the ports are closed because of a strike, on the other, because of ice conditions. It is possible to solve both problems provided we can discuss them and arrive at a decision.
That is why I believe the matter is pressing, for winter will soon set in.
You are undoubtedly aware, Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as your home is close to the St. Lawrence seaway, that according to the latest news the St. Lawrence seaway will be closed tomorrow morning for fear of a freeze-up in the next few days. Under those circumstances, I feel the matter is urgent. If we wait another week, our winter navigation may be a failure, and the shipping companies in Europe, South America and Africa, which might otherwise be interested in shipping by way of the St. Lawrence, may not do so because of the recent statement of the Department of Transport. For that reason, I would ask you to allow debate on this urgent and important matter of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence.

It is the view of the government that social security leg'slation should include a right of appeal for applicants for benefits under the program and for beneficiaries. Where a difference of opinion arises between the administrat.on on the one hand and a dissatisfied person on the other as to the amount of benefit being pa;d or the eligibility of the applicant there should be a means whereby an inexpensive and impartial review and determination of the question can be carried out.
The unemployment insurance legislation passed by parliament more than 25 years ago made such provision. The Canada Pension Plan passed by the house last year and the Canada Assistance Plan passed earlier this year each contain a provision to ensure the right of appeal. We believe it is important that th;s basic right be included in the program. This is all that is involved in the provision of the right to appeal. It is in accordance with the practice imbedded in the Unemployment Insurance Act, the Canada Pension Plan and the Canada Assistance Plan. Now it will be applicable to the Old Age Security Act.
The old age security regulations now provide for the establishment of tribunals from

Old Age Security Act Amendment time to time to whom the minister may refer for final decision questions arising as to the age of an applicant or pensioner. I will conclude by repeating the justification for this program. This program is intended to give help where it is needed most to persons on low or modest incomes. On this ground I believe it is a superior program and I believe it will be regarded as such by those old age pensioners who are living now only on old age security.
The second point about this program is that it gives help where it is needed most by redistributing income in this direction. It does so in the future because it is a transitional program which places a reducing burden on the federal treasury owing to the fact that it will gradually work its way out of existence as the Canada and Quebec pension plans come into full fruition.
We are doing this without the application of the much dreaded and odious means test. There is no possible comparison between the simple declaration which must be filled out merely asking applicants to list items of income under the Income Tax Act, and a means test. It merely asks the old age pensioners to fill out a simple form listing the items of income which they would normally list if they were filing an income tax return. I see no indignity or loss of self-respect in the process. That is what we are standing on. It is a humane test, admitted as such by the Canadian Welfare Council. There is an element missing here, and it is one which is essential with respect to the legislation offered to this house and to the country as containing the elements of the national transportation policy needed to provide a better and fairer means of carrying goods and people between all parts of Canada.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
In offering this amendment to clause 1, which I understand is an indication to the commission to be established of the extent it should take into account a number of factors,

I do so because as I indicated earlier this commission will be venturing into uncharted courses like a spaceman reaching for one of the planets. It will come up against problems which it never has contemplated and which I am sure neither the minister nor those persons who drafted this bill have considered. All one needs to support this is to look at the report of proceedings and evidence of the committee. It is my belief that the element which is mentioned in this bill is one which has been the subject matter of a great number of directions. It has been the basis for inquiries made heretofore over a great number of years. I am speaking of the direction that the board have responsibilitiy for regulating and setting freight rates to provide for as great a measure of equalization as is possible within the very difficult circumstances which we have in this country because of the matters of geography and economies.
I do not care what is done; you cannot escape the fact that there is going to be some inequity and some discrimination. It will be impossible to reach that measure of equalization which we would like to see. Perfection in this aspect of our problems is not at all possible. I readily accede to that. However, under the existing law which we are to replace to some extent there were some attempts to eliminate this inequity and bring about equalization. I am referring to section 336 of the present Railway Act which, of course, will be eliminated by the provision we are now making.
A very brief historial record I think will help to place my views before the committee and indicate the reasons I am moving this amendment. In 1925 order in council P.C. 886 was passed by which the Board of Transport Commissioners was directed by the government to examine the freight rate structure and attempt to bring in harmony and provide for a measure of equity in all parts and regions of Canada. Later, in 1948, by order in council P.C. 1487, there was a further direction by the then government to the Board of Transport Commissioners.
The board of transport commissioners, in taking this responsibility, required a number of years to report. I do not think it was until some time in 1955 that they filed their report. At that time they made a statement which was quite correct. They said that equalization in Canada involved the establishment of a fundamental base and a statistical survey which would take many years of study to complete. The board of transport commissioners proceeded some distance along this

I think we are in agreement. As you know, rates are set for a certain product in a certain area, and no one ever examines them from year to year. These discriminatory rate structures remain for ever and ever. I was hoping this amendment would make it clear to the Canadian Transport Commission that their job is to try to set rates wherever possible on the basis of equalization, rather than on the basis of phraseology contained in clause 68, which deals with section 381 (1).
The other point I wish to make is that I think it is wrong in principle to worship the theory of competition to such a degree that you give to a private company, whether it is the C.P.R., the C.N.R. or the P.G.E., the right to decide what the freight rate will be for a certain new development as opposed to another new development. This, in the name of competition, gives too much power to the private company. If the Canadian Transport Commission were on the alert for this type of thing, it could be prevented. One can imagine that, with the interlocking directorates, and with the C.P.R. which is engaged in many forms of enterprise, if one of these enterprises belonged to the circle of their companies and another set of enterprises belonged to the competitive company, discrimination could occur.
I do not want to impute bad motives or to suggest that the railway would deliberately set a special rate to help their boys a little bit more than the others, but I would like to believe there was a referee or a judicial court set up to stop this sort of thing, unless there were good reasons for establishing lower rates at one point than at another. The principle

should remain, that similar goods travelling the same distances should be treated in the same way.
In the case of the oil and gas industry, we do not bother with these details in legislation. Mr. Speaker, let me say at the outset that the government shares the concern of the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Laprise) concerning the communities in this country, and more particularly those in northwestern Quebec, which are dependant upon the gold mining industry. To this extent the government is considering the continuation beyond December 31, 1967, of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. The Department of Industry of course is concerned with the development of other industries in those areas, and the new manpower centres are operating in such a way as to retrain and redirect labour to new occupations as they develop in the gold mining regions.
The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was passed in 1948. As the name indicates, the problems then confronting the gold mining industry were thought to be transitional in nature; this was an emergency measure. It has continued over the intervening years and the amount of assistance has increased. For example, the amount of assistance increased from $580 per miner per annum in the mid-1950's to a figure in the order of $1,400 per miner per annum in 1966. The total extent of federal tax assistance to the gold mining industry this year will be in the order of $15 million. The industry is declining in output. Paced with a fixed price for its products and rising costs, particularly rising wage rates, it has been in a squeeze. It has done a remarkable job in respect of improving productivity. In general the number of mines in this country has dropped roughly in half since 1948. The problem in northwestern Quebec is not unique. It is a problem which is being encountered in Ontario, British Columbia and in other parts of the country. I know there are other mining opportunities in that general area. The other mining industries are able today to pay something in the order of $20 a week more, and they are drawing off mining labour from the gold mines. Pulp and paper and other industries are in that area.
Nevertheless, the government is prepared to continue the emergency gold mining assistance in some form. It is also energetically exploring the possibility of other opportunities for employment in adjoining areas to support these communities in the future.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a brief word about an aspect of this clause which is of great interest to southwestern Ontario. As the minister knows, for some years there has been concern in southwestern Ontario about the freight rates for shipping goods from our part of Canada to other parts of the country. Rates for shipments to eastern Canada have been based on a mileage basis and therefore lower rates were being paid from places like Toronto and Montreal to the maritimes than from Windsor. The rates for shipments to the west, however, are based on block rates and shippers from southwestern Ontario have not been able to get rates based on the shorter mileage through the United States to western Canada. The geographical situation, while reflected in ratemaking to eastern Canada, has not in the past been equally reflected in rates to western Canada from southwestern Ontario.
This problem has been brought to the attention of various governments of different parties and to various royal commissions on transportation by the southwestern Ontario chambers of commerce and particularly the Windsor, Ontario, chamber of commerce on a number of occasions in the past. I myself have raised this matter in the house both when the previous Conservative government was in office and later after our own Liberal party formed the government. I think it is a departure from the usual practice to raise a matter of this type before knowing exactly what would be the attitude of one's own party. In these circumstances one often finds that members who raise such matters when they were in the opposition do not do so when their party is in government. However, I departed from this practice and brought this matter to the attention of my government in the house. Since that particular occasion I have remained in direct contact with the minister and his department on this important matter.
The freight traffic committee of the Windsor chamber of commerce decided to present a
January 16, 1967

further brief on this problem to the transport committee of the house while it was studying Bill C-231. It suggested that the freight rate problem in southwestern Ontario could be at least partially solved by a certain amendment to the wording of section 325 which is covered by clause 48 of the bill. I might add that I met with the Windsor freight traffic committee in Windsor to discuss the proposed brief with them before they appeared before the transport committee and in fact assisted them in making arrangements for their appearance before this particular committee of the house.
When the bill was reported to the house the transport committee did not recommend the particular changes to clause 48 requested by the Windsor freight traffic group. Since 1963 the Windsor area and southwestern Ontario generally have benefited from an unparalleled period of economic growth and development. I think that the policies of the present government, particularly the designated area program and the auto pact, have had a lot to do with this. The need for certain changes in the legislation governing freight rates would have appeared more significant had these other government policies which I have mentioned not worked as well as they did. However, more equitable treatment for southwestern Ontario with regard to freight rates would certainly be helpful in assuring the continuing economic health of our area. It deserves some improvement in its presently existing freight rate situation.
As the government has apparently not accepted the specific form of amendment to this clause proposed by the Windsor chamber of commerce to the transportation committee, I ask the minister to indicate just how this bill can be of assistance to southwestern Ontario. It may be that the specific amendment sought by the Windsor chamber of commerce would have been better suited to the regulatory approach of the previously existing legislation which the bill before us is designed to replace and therefore does not fit in with the different philosophy of rate-making and transportation policy which underlies the proposed legislation. It may be that the minister and the department feel that the aim of the Windsor chamber of commerce to get more equitable treatment in freight rates for southwestern Ontario shippers is in fact being met in the present bill although in a different manner from that specifically sought by it. If that is so may I ask the minister to indicate specifically how this is being done.

The hon. gentleman is repeating a phrase which two or three of his

hon. friends have used. I have the impression that notwithstanding the fact that I have tried several times to correct it, my efforts have been completely without success. Let me repeat: There is no intention whatever, indeed it is forbidden in this bill, to review the Crowsnest rates. They are frozen as hard as any legislation could possibly freeze them, for all time to come. We have even improved the situation by freezing them specifically for Churchill.
The review has to do with the cost of moving this grain, and nothing else. The review will not endanger the Crowsnest rates in any way whatsoever; in fact, it will safeguard them, and if hon. gentlemen opposite are right in believing that the rates are compensatory, the sooner someone can establish that contention objectively, the better, because then nobody could attack the rates. This is what we are seeking to accomplish.
I am just a little resentful of the implication in the speeches from members opposite that I

and all I have ever done in this house has been to strengthen the Crowsnest rates-am trying in some insidious way to get rid of them. I am doing the exact opposite. But I think the Canadian people are entitled to know what the position really is, since a royal commission appointed by the Leader of the Opposition said that these rates are not compensatory. We do not accept that view, but we do not say the reverse. All we say is that within three years an objective commission must find out what the facts are. If they reach a certain conclusion, they can recommend that a certain payment be made to the railways so that we can safeguard the Crowsnest rates. That is what we are trying to do. When the Meighen government destroyed them after the first world war, the Liberal government brought them back.
I am getting tired of this situation which is developing in the committee. The only time in the history of this country when there was any attack on the Crowsnest rates was after the first world war, and the attack was made by a Conservative government. I think they learned their lesson. We are trying to embed these rates as firmly as we can in the constitution. But hon. members should bear in mind that these rates are the only rates which have guaranteed almost in perpetuity in the whole freight structure in this country in favour of western farmers. All we are saying is that if these rates are not compensatory the treasury should pay for the difference, and not the other freight shippers in the rest of Canada. Surely, this is a reasonable position to take. It
January 17, 1967

is surely not fair for the eastern farmers or for the fishermen of the Atlantic provinces, or for the people of British Columbia to be expected to pay higher freight rates in order to maintain the Crowsnest rates for the benefit of western farmers. If the Crowsnest rates do not themselves pay the costs, then the treasury should make up the difference. That is all this bill says-absolutely all it says. It does not say they are not compensatory.
I think that if hon. gentlemen opposite had the faith they pretend to have, they would not be a bit afraid of this review. The only thing one can conclude from their desperate fear of this review is that they do not really believe what they themselves are saying. If they really believed that the railways are now making money moving grain, why are they worried about having the facts made known to the public? There should not be any concern on their part if the rates are compensatory. The only reason for them to be worried would be if they were not-and I do not understand what worry there would be, then, because the legislation practically says that if the rates are not compensatory the treasury should make up the difference. That is all there is to it, and I think it is about time we faced the facts as they are in the legislation. I have tried to be patient about this and I intend to continue being very patient, but it is hard to go on and on hearing members opposite say the direct opposite of what the plain English in this bill is saying.

Yet, despite the fact that there have been many radical and fundamental changes in western Canada's economy since those explosive years, the system of grain handling established before the first world war-the collection, storage and transport of the prairie grain crop-has changed very little.

Mr. Chairman, I should like very briefly to put to the minister the suggestion that even though the amendment just proposed to subsection 1 of new section 336 has been defeated, it is still not too late to make other improvements to the section so it
January 20, 1967

will be more fair in its effect and more effective. I suggest to the minister that even if he did not see fit to accept the amendment which would have given a more comprehensive definition to the term "captive shipper," that is one thing; but he should still give serious thought to the formula itself which will be applied by the commission in giving some protection to those, presumably very few, shippers who will be regarded as captive under the terms of this legislation.
Obviously, under subsection 2 of new section 336 the formula is that the commission shall set as a maximum a rate determined by taking the variable cost to the railways and adding 150 per cent to that variable cost. The rate shall be determined in this way. It was aptly demonstrated yesterday by other speakers and myself that it is very possible, in fact likely, that the railways, in the majority of cases where they are hauling commodities shipped by captive shippers, will be enjoying a mark-up in the order of 300 per cent and 400 per cent. I say this because the maximum rate formula, based as it is on variable cost plus 150 per cent and determined from a standard of a 30,000 pounds carload lot, will mean that in instances where the haulage is in carload lots of 70,000 pounds, 80,000 pounds,
90,000	pounds, 100,000 pounds or heavier, the mark-up will in fact be 300 per cent or 400 per cent.
In no case these days do the railways haul commodities in full carload lots of a weight less than 60,000 pounds or 70,000 pounds. When we look at the table given to the committee by the Manitoba council, and by Professors Williams and Borts, we find that the mark-up of the railways when they are hauling, under this formula, 70,000 pounds or 80,060 pounds carload lots is, as I said and I repeat again and again, in the order of 300 per cent, 400 per cent or even more. To have a maximum rate formula which allows for this kind of mark-up is simply incredible; there is no other word to describe it. It is unacceptable in every respect.
I hope the minister will see fit to accept the proposition that the formula ought to be changed so that the mark-up of the railways, when hauling goods for captive shippers, will be of an order that is deemed reasonable, just and permissible. A mark-up that is hovering around 300 per cent and 400 per cent is certainly not reasonable or just, and should not be regarded as permissible by members of this committee who are here to protect the public
Transportation
interest and the interest of shippers, particularly those shippers who are captive to the railways because of location or any other circumstance.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in order to bring this matter to a head and get the sense of members of the committee, I move:
That clause 336 subclause (2) be amended by deleting the words "150 per cent of the variable cost as the fixed rate applicable to the carriage of the goods" in lines 21 and 22 and substituting the following: "the percentage difference that total permissive earnings are to freight variable costs plus an amount computed as being the cost of capital applicable to the carriage of such goods."
Speaking to the amendment, I wish to say that if accepted it would do two things. It would remove this fictitious formula which, as I have already said, would have the effect of giving the railways the opportunity to derive unconscionable mark-ups-and I think that is the proper word-on the carriage of commodities hauled for captive shippers. In addition, it would remove what I consider to be a rather basic anomaly in this section. The basic anomaly, in my opinion, is that under the terms of this formula the railways will be able to consider the cost of capital to be a variable cost and will be able to obtain a mark-up of 150 per cent on the cost of capital. The railways are not in the banking business, and it seems to me strange that they should be able to take advantage of a formula to actually make money on money. I thought this was a function of our banking institutions and not our transportation companies.
If the cost of money is to be computed into variable cost, that is fine; but the railways should not be allowed to earn a mark-up of 150 per cent, and it may be even more, on the cost of money to them. To try and articulate this point a little more precisely I would say that the cost of the money to the railways, which is deemed to be part of their variable cost, should be treated in this way; the railways should be allowed to recover the cost of money to them, but they should not be allowed to charge a rate that will give them 150 per cent of the cost of money to them. If my amendment were accepted it would remove this anomaly.
During the committee stage and the ensuing discussion in this chamber I did not hear the minister put forward any defence of the proposition that the cost of money to the railways should be brought into this formula so the railways could receive a return of 150 per cent of the cost of money to them.

We do not say to a wheat farmer that he should be allowed to make only a reasonable profit. He can make just as much profit as is possible in all the circumstances. I admit that most of the time it is not adequate. Still there is no law which limits it. Also, there is no law limiting what profit the International Nickel Company can make, what profit the sulphur producers can make or what profit the potash companies can make. In the case of these exporters we say they should sell their product for all that the traffic will bear, because this helps our balance of payments. We want them to do this.
In the competitive sector it seems we are telling the railways that we do not want to be handing out millions of dollars to them in the form of subsidies. I think many of us, because we are adults or old men like I am, have formed our habits when we were young and therefore do not realize that today the Canadian railways do not have anything like the bargaining power they had in the period between the first and second world wars and in the period before the first world war. Had the situation not changed, there would have been no justification for the whole MacPherson approach to this matter. Speech:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday, January 12 the hon. member for Skeena raised a question of privilege in connection with notice of motion for the production of papers No. 191.
I have investigated the complaints made by the hon. member on that occasion and again yesterday, and I should like to apologize on behalf of the C.B.C. for the misunderstanding which led the hon. member to raise his question of privilege. The C.B.C. erroneously understood that the motion applied only to correspondence between the C.B.C. and other employers not associated with the corporation. This information was conveyed to the hon. member in perfectly good faith by my colleague the Associate Minister of National Defence on January 11. I regret the confusion this situation created.
As to the notice of motion for the production of papers, the C.B.C. has submitted that it has not been customary to require the corporation to produce such correspondence which is basically related to its detailed management and administration, and for that reason had not considered such correspondence was covered by the motion.
Since I have a ministerial responsibility to report for the C.B.C. I wish to express to the hon. member for Skeena and to the house my regrets for this inadvertent situation which has arisen.

Mr. Speaker, whether the government is aware of it or not this country is facing a housing crisis. The proposal the minister has announced today is about as adequate to meet the housing crisis as it would be to feed a peanut to an elephant in the hope of assuaging its hunger. The proposal the minister has outlined to make direct loans to the builders to enable them to construct some 20,000 housing units certainly will be of help to the builders, but it will be of little assistance to the people who really need houses and who are in the moderate income brackets.
As the minister himself has admitted, one would need an income of $8,000 or more per annum in order to buy a house today. The latest figures show that a house which cost $25,000 in 1966 could have been purchased in 1965 for $20,000. The cost of property is going up, and the housing program the minister has announced will benefit mainly those persons whose incomes are such that they can afford to pay the very large price that is involved here.
My colleagues the hon. member for Dan-forth and the hon. member for Broadview have been urging the minister over the past two or three years to announce a housing

policy of direct loans to persons desirous of becoming home owners and not just to builders; that is, to the people in the middle income groups. The government is in a position to borrow money at much lower rates than the average individual can borrow money even under the National Housing Act. Unless the government is prepared to make very large sums of money available to prospective home owners by means of direct loans, the people in the middle income groups are not going to be in a position to buy or build homes.
We hope the government will take some cognizance of the request that homes be made available, by means of direct lending, without a down payment and at low interest rates. We hope some such action will be taken to reduce the cost to those people who want to buy lots.

The last report carried in the Toronto Daily Star indicated that people in the metropolitan Toronto area were paying as much as $10,000 per lot. That price makes it prohibitive for individuals with incomes of $4,000, $5,000 or $6,000 per year to purchase homes.
We have been urging the government, and urge them again, to embark upon a large scale public housing program which will make homes available to a great number of Canadians who today have no hope of owning homes under the present provisions of the N.H.A. It is not enough for the minister to compare housing starts and housing completions with those of 1965. Under present circumstances there has to be a greatly accelerated program. It is estimated that something over a million new homes are needed in Canada. The present tepid and inadequate approach will not give very much encouragement to those Canadian people who are looking for homes in which to live. There is little value in having an affluent society when at the same time thousands of young couples have no means to build houses in which to live and raise families.
We hope the government will make some announcement very soon in respect of a housing policy rather than give us bits and pieces which, added together, indicate that it really has no policy and no imaginative approach to this very serious housing crisis.

It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the most important issue in this debate is whether or not the present legislation, which we are told is designed to unify our armed forces, really indicates an important shift in our foreign and defence policies and, if it does, whether this shift in our foreign and defence policies is desirable. To date the government and, indeed, various organizations have dragged in a number of red herrings, so to speak, which have thoroughly confused the real issues involved. aspects of this bill but it does appear, despite all the confusion, that the following are to be essential elements of the measure.
First, it is the intention of the government to set up a single service which will be outfitted in one kind of uniform the design of which has apparently not yet been chosen and that all designations of rank will be an agglomeration of those now used in the existing services. It also appears that the government intends to do this over a number of years, perhaps over three or four years.
Second, it would appear that the new service will be extremely mobile and well armed. To this extent it will probably be very efficient. It will resemble a kind of marine corps or possibly, as somebody put it, a modified police force. I suppose it will rather resemble a marine corps.
Third, it appears that the air force and the navy will eventually be relegated largely to transport and support roles. These three considerations seem to emerge from the morass of information which has been handed out. As has already been pointed out this afternoon, the minister's public relations men are already organized upstairs, passing out information on this program to the press gallery. It is difficult for members of this house to compete with such a formidable tribe because they probably have easier access to the press than do most of us. However, I rely on the judgment of the members of the press gallery to pay some attention eventually to the arguments put forward in this house as well as to those handed out to them by the minister's public relations staff. I understand the director of the National Parks Branch has acknowledged your letter-

Let me pause there to say that a new lease will be granted, but this gentleman must give up a 21 year period of renewal.

When Mr. Gourlay submitted his plans to the department they were ignored. What happened after he commenced that action? Mr. Speaker, my colleague has asked a most interesting question. This is done before second reading. I understand that in all cases the actual second reading is left to parliament itself. In other words, parliament can either accept or reject the recommendation for second reading made by this committee, so that parliament's rights are properly protected.
My reading of literature on parliamentary reform tells me, Mr. Speaker, that two rather simple steps have been taken. The first one was in the early 1880's the other in 1902. Until the 1880's it had been felt that parliament should be untrammelled and everyone bowed to freedom of speech and other shibboleths. Parliament had to face an interesting group of members from Ireland who used every device and delaying action to hold up parliament. As is usual when challenged, parliament found a means of using freedom of speech to its proper end. In other words, Mr. Speaker, these proposals have had historical origins, and I am intrigued to think that the trouble encountered by the Irish M.P.'s really instituted the first great procedural reform in the British House of Commons.
However, we in Canada have not had that experience so our rules, with very little variation, are the rules that we adopted prior to the reforms which took place in Britain in the 1880's. There are, of course, certain exceptions, and we can all think of them. That is why I plead with the government to take the initiative in re-establishing as a standing committee the committee on procedure, because reform is not a matter that should be handled piecemeal.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, if reform is to be anything more than just a matter for discussion by members of parliament

DEBATES	February 7, 1967
throughout the country we should examine the fundamental reasons behind each and every one of our rules. Perhaps a case can be made, as it was made in Australia, for abandoning the committee of ways and means procedure. Perhaps a case can be made for, shall I say, having a slightly more disciplined question period. Perhaps a case can also be made-I think it can

for reducing the number of members on committees, reducing the quorums, and widening the scope of the responsibilities that those committees are called upon to undertake.
In last month's issue of "Encounter" there is an article by Mr. Henry Fairlie. In it we are reminded of a phrase used by Mr. R. A. Butler-"the patience of politics". Mr. Fairlie
says:
The phrase is R. A. Butler's. It expresses, more vividly than any other single phrase, the character of politics in a free country.
In the politician, it demands that he should accustom himself to the inevitable fluctuations of political fortunes; that he should And defeat and failure only an invitation to renewed efforts; that he should overcome the galling frustrations of enforced idleness and opposition, and be able to look forward to ten years in the wilderness with equanimity and self-assurance.
That is something from which a good many of us would profit if we took it to heart.
It demands that he should never try to seize imaginary initiatives or seek speedy results; that he should wait calmly for his opportunity; that he should never despair or panic.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
It demands that he should bear obloquy, misrepresentation, and injuries without complaint; that he should expect no gratitude; that he should remain silent when one word would justify him, if that word would injure his cause. Above all, It demands that he should never, whatever the provocation, cease to trust in the right instincts of a free people; that he should believe always In their ability, in the long run, to distinguish truth from falsehood, justice, from injustice, the sound from the meretricious; that he should, in this belief, patiently pursue the task of bringing different ideas and interests into contact with each other, never doubting that the arts of a free government are among the most rewarding of all the arts of a civilised people.
We have a responsibility to so enlarge the scope of this chamber and the character, if I may use that word, and attributes of its members that our people may indeed believe we are good practitioners of the art of politics.
